summary:
Ingushetia stands under the framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that also bears on foreign visitors.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex", including speech that justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. Within 48 hours of the 2023 ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night; arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, while the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

At the regional level the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 "extremist" designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreign nationals and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since January 2024, organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as "extremist". The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.
tangentialFactors:
Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented within the Russian framework. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had had found. Family-initiated detention of this kind is a documented mechanism alongside state action.

The North Caucasus is assessed differently from the rest of Russia by the UK Home Office, which otherwise finds no general persecution basis for LGBT+ claims involving Russia; Ingushetia therefore sits in the one regional category where an asylum claim on gender identity or LGBT+ advocacy is assessed as likely to succeed on persecution grounds. The same note records that violence now spreads beyond the region, so the regional finding does not confine exposure to the North Caucasus itself.

Global Affairs Canada's travel advice for Russia combines a blanket avoid-all-travel warning with a specific terrorism listing for Ingushetia, Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai, and separately records surveillance of foreign nationals. The 2SLGBTQI+ attack language in the advisory is national in scope rather than specific to Ingushetia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ingushetia live under the Russian prohibition on legal gender recognition, the ban on gender reassignment surgery and the associated restriction on changing gender markers on official documents. Gender-affirming surgical care is unavailable lawfully.

Marriages concluded by trans persons with someone of their same birth sex are void under the 2023 law, and people diagnosed with gender dysphoria lose the right to adopt. These consequences fall on residents as well as on anyone present in the territory.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The state does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, so residents cannot rely on recorded statistics or aggravated-penalty provisions.

The propaganda provisions apply to resident speech as well as to material aimed at minors, and the extremism designation exposes residents to administrative and criminal charges for displaying rainbow symbols. Regional conditions described by North Caucasus SOS include detention and forced return to families arising from private existence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Ingushetia-specific figures for extremism convictions, propaganda-law prosecutions or fines; those enforcement totals are national Russian figures and cannot be attributed to this republic.

No source in the inventory documents a specific killing of a trans person in Ingushetia, nor names a local detention facility, prosecution or court ruling in the territory. Regional findings are carried by the UK Home Office note and the North Caucasus SOS interview rather than by Ingushetia-specific reporting.

The Global Affairs Canada advisory does not specify which areas require Ministry of Interior special permission, so the geographic scope of that requirement within Ingushetia is unresolved.

Whether the UK Home Office regional persecution finding affects protection for a trans visitor detained inside Russia, as opposed to an asylum claim made to UK authorities, is not addressed in the inventory.
